title: MARY MAGDALENE IS NEVER CALLED A PROSTITUTE IN THE BIBLE—So Where Did That Idea Come From?
paragraphs: MARY MAGDALENE IS NEVER CALLED A PROSTITUTE IN THE BIBLE—So Where Did That Idea Come From?

For centuries, millions have remembered her for a sexual past the Bible never gives her. But when you remove the legend and actually listen to Scripture, Mary Magdalene’s real story may be even more powerful—and far more personal—than the one many of us were taught.
There is something unsettling about discovering that a story you have heard your entire life is not actually in the Bible.
Not misunderstood.
Not poorly translated.
Not hidden somewhere in an obscure verse.
Simply...
not there.
Ask many Christians who Mary Magdalene was, and the answer comes almost automatically:
“She was a prostitute whom Jesus forgave.”
Paintings have portrayed her that way.
Films have portrayed her that way.
Sermons have sometimes portrayed her that way.
Popular imagination has wrapped her in the familiar image of the sexually fallen woman who encountered Jesus, repented, and became one of His devoted followers.
It is certainly a dramatic redemption story.
There is only one problem.
The Bible never calls Mary Magdalene a prostitute.
Not once.
Matthew does not.
Mark does not.
Luke does not.
John does not.

There is no verse saying Mary Magdalene sold her body. No Gospel identifies her as an adulteress. No apostle tells us she lived a sexually immoral life. Scripture never even identifies her as the unnamed sinful woman who washed Jesus’ feet with her tears.
And once you realize that, something almost uncomfortable happens.
You have to meet Mary again.
Not the Mary created by centuries of accumulated tradition.
The Mary standing inside the pages of Scripture.
And perhaps that matters more than we realize, because Mary Magdalene is not the only person who has ever lived beneath a story other people attached to her.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe somebody still remembers you by the worst season of your life.
Maybe your family has a version of you.
Your former friends have another.
Your church has another.
Your past has another.
Maybe people heard one chapter and decided they knew the entire book.
And perhaps that is why Mary Magdalene's story reaches beyond an ancient historical misunderstanding.
Because sometimes people remember a scandal Jesus never wrote.
Sometimes human beings attach identities that God did not.
And sometimes grace begins by letting Jesus tell the truth about who you are.
Luke introduces Mary Magdalene by name in Luke 8. The Greek text reads:
“Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει.”
Maria hē kaloumenē Magdalēnē, aph’ hēs daimonia hepta exelēlythei.
Mary, the one called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out.
That is what Luke tells us.
Seven demons.
Not seven lovers.
Not prostitution.
Not adultery.
Not sexual immorality.
Demons.
Think about that.
The woman remembered in popular culture as a prostitute appears in Scripture as a woman whom Jesus had delivered—and who then became part of a group materially supporting His ministry.
Her biblical introduction is not primarily about sexual scandal.
It is about deliverance.
It is about discipleship.
It is about generosity.
It is about what happens when somebody who has experienced the power of Christ decides that what she possesses can now serve the mission of Christ.
And that changes the picture considerably.
We should also be careful about something else.
Having seven demons does not give us permission to invent seven particular sins.
Demonic oppression or possession in the Gospels is not synonymous with prostitution. Scripture simply does not provide the missing biography our curiosity may want.
There are things about Mary's life before Jesus that God chose not to tell us.
Perhaps there is humility in leaving them there.
We do not honor Scripture by filling its silences with rumors.
But then how did the prostitute story become so famous?
To understand that, you have to notice what happens immediately before Mary appears in Luke's Gospel.
At the end of Luke 7, Jesus is eating in the home of a Pharisee named Simon when an unnamed woman enters.
Luke describes her with the Greek expression:
“γυνὴ ... ἁμαρτωλός”
gunē ... hamartōlos—
a woman who was a sinner.
She weeps.
Her tears fall onto Jesus’ feet.
She wipes them with her hair.
She kisses His feet.
She anoints them.
Simon watches and silently questions Jesus because of the woman's reputation.
Jesus responds with one of the most beautiful lessons about forgiveness in the Gospel and finally tells the woman that her sins are forgiven and that her faith has saved her (Luke 7:36–50).
It is an extraordinary scene.
But read it carefully.
Luke never says:
“Her name was Mary Magdalene.”
The woman is unnamed.
Then Luke 8 begins, and Mary Magdalene is named among the women associated with Jesus’ ministry.
Because the stories appear close together, later interpreters connected them.
But proximity is not identity.
Then another Mary entered the picture.
Mary of Bethany.
She was the sister of Martha and Lazarus (John 11:1–2). John later describes Mary of Bethany anointing Jesus’ feet with expensive perfume and wiping them with her hair (John 12:1–8).
Now the similarities seemed irresistible.
An unnamed sinful woman anoints Jesus.
Mary of Bethany anoints Jesus.
Mary Magdalene appears immediately after Luke's account of the sinful woman and had been delivered from seven demons.
Over time, in Western Christian tradition, three identities became intertwined.
The unnamed sinful woman.
Mary of Bethany.
Mary Magdalene.
One of the most influential moments in this development came in A.D. 591, when Pope Gregory the Great preached what is known as Homily 33.

Gregory identified the sinful woman in Luke with the Mary mentioned by John and with the Mary from whom seven demons had been cast out. He interpreted those seven demons symbolically as representing the fullness of vice and connected the woman's former use of perfume with forbidden behavior.
That interpretation became enormously influential in Western Christianity.
But notice the distinction.
Gregory was interpreting.
Luke was reporting.
And those are not the same thing.
The Bible says Mary Magdalene had been delivered from seven demons.
It does not say those demons represented seven sexual sins.
The Bible describes an unnamed woman in Luke 7 as sinful.
It does not name her Mary Magdalene.
And even Luke's description of that unnamed woman as hamartōlos—a sinner—does not itself identify her occupation as prostitution.
In later Western imagination, however, the identities increasingly blended until Mary Magdalene became the great archetype of the repentant sexually immoral woman.
The irony is almost painful.
Because when we allow Scripture itself to tell Mary's story, the emphasis falls somewhere very different.
Follow her through the Gospel narratives.
When Jesus is crucified, Mary Magdalene is there.
When His body is buried, Mary Magdalene is associated with the women watching and remembering.
When the Sabbath has passed and hope seems buried behind a stone, Mary Magdalene goes toward the tomb.
And then comes one of the most breathtaking moments in all Scripture.
John 20.
It is still dark.
Mary arrives at the tomb.
The stone has been moved.
She runs.
She tells Peter and the other disciple.
They come.
They see.
Eventually they leave.
But Mary stays.
Crying.
That detail should stop us.
Everybody else can leave.
Mary stays near the place where she thinks Jesus' body should be.
She has already experienced deliverance from darkness once.
Now it feels as though darkness has swallowed everything again.
Her Teacher is dead.
His body appears to be missing.
Her world has collapsed twice.
First at Golgotha.
Now at an empty tomb she does not yet understand.
She bends down.
She sees angels.
Then she turns and sees Jesus—but does not recognize Him.
She assumes He is the gardener.
Jesus asks why she is crying and whom she is seeking.
Mary begs Him to tell her where the body has been taken.
And then...
one word.
Her name.
The Greek of John 20:16 preserves the moment with almost unbearable simplicity:
“λέγει αὐτῇ Ἰησοῦς· Μαριάμ.”
Legei autē Iēsous: Mariam.
Jesus says to her:
“Mary.”
That is it.
He says her name.
And the world changes.
She turns toward Him and cries:
“Ῥαββουνί!”
Rabbouni!
Teacher.
The word is Aramaic in origin, preserved for us inside John's Greek Gospel.
Imagine the sound of that moment.
She had watched Him die.
She had wept beside an empty tomb.
She thought His body had been stolen.
Then the risen Jesus called her by name.
Mary.
Not prostitute.
Not scandal.
Not damaged woman.
Not the label centuries of people would eventually place upon her.
Mary.
There are moments when grace does not need a paragraph.
It only needs Jesus to call your name.
Maybe that is why this story hurts in such a beautiful way.
Because some of us have spent years answering to names Jesus never gave us.
Failure.
Addict.
Dirty.
Rejected.
Divorced.
Unwanted.
Hypocrite.
Ruined.
Unlovable.
Backslider.
Too far gone.
People said it.
Maybe you said it about yourself.
Perhaps your sin really was terrible.
Perhaps unlike the invented scandal attached to Mary Magdalene, your scandal is painfully real.
The Gospel does not require us to pretend otherwise.
Christianity is not salvation through reputation management.
Scripture says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
We do not need Mary Magdalene to have been a prostitute for grace to be amazing.
We already need grace ourselves.
That is the deeper danger of the old stereotype.
If we turn Mary into an exaggerated sinner merely so Jesus can look like an exaggerated Savior, we have misunderstood both sin and grace.
Jesus does not need us to manufacture someone's darkness to make His light impressive.
The cross is already enough.
Our sin is already real.
His mercy is already astonishing.
And whatever Mary's seven demons meant experientially, this much Scripture makes clear:
Jesus delivered her.
Her bondage did not get the final word.
And after being delivered, she followed.
She gave.
She stayed.
She witnessed.
She went.
That is a Gospel-shaped life.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past is forgiven.”
Grace says, “Come follow Me.”
Grace does not merely pull us out of darkness.
Grace brings us into discipleship.
Grace does not merely erase condemnation.
Grace redirects the life that has been redeemed.
And perhaps the most beautiful reversal comes after the resurrection.
Mary arrives grieving over a dead Jesus.
She leaves announcing a living Christ.
John 20:18 records her testimony:
“I have seen the Lord.”
Think about those words.
The woman whom later generations would so often remember primarily through an alleged sexual scandal is remembered by the Gospel itself as a witness proclaiming the risen Christ.

In 2016, even the Roman Catholic Church's official decree elevating Mary Magdalene's liturgical celebration described her as the first witness of the Lord's resurrection and first evangelist, while an accompanying Vatican explanation highlighted the historic title associated with her:
“apostle of the apostles.”
What a reversal.
History often remembered the alleged scandal.
Scripture leads us toward the witness.
And isn't that exactly what Jesus does?
People remember what you were.
Jesus knows what grace is making you.
People keep replaying Friday.
Jesus walks out of the tomb on Sunday.
People point toward your chains.
Jesus points toward the empty place where those chains fell.
This does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Far from it.
Jesus Christ did not die so we could rename sin and continue living comfortably inside it.
The cross declares simultaneously that our sin is worse than our excuses admit and that God's grace is greater than our shame can imagine.
Repentance means turning toward God.
Grace means discovering that the Savior toward whom you turn has already stretched out wounded hands to receive sinners.
The Gospel is not:
“You were never bad.”
The Gospel is:
Christ is good enough to save the guilty.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives forgiveness and eternal life—not because they repaired themselves, but because Jesus saves.
Mary's story therefore should not become an excuse to say, “See, she wasn't really sinful.”
She was human.
She needed Christ.
So do we.
The correction is not that Mary was too good to need grace.
The correction is that we do not have permission to invent sins Scripture never assigns to her.
That distinction matters.
Because truth matters.
And because Christians of all people should understand the danger of false labels.
Maybe someone reading this right now has been imprisoned by one.
Maybe the accusation was true.
Maybe it was false.
Maybe it was partly true and cruelly exaggerated.
Maybe people met you during your worst year and never updated their picture of you.
Maybe you repented, but they still introduce you emotionally by your old life.
Maybe Jesus forgave something that you keep dragging back into the courtroom.
Hear the Gospel.
Your hope is not that your past never happened.
Your hope is that Jesus Christ entered human history precisely to redeem sinners.
At the cross, He bore judgment.
In the grave, He entered death.
On the third day, He rose victorious.
And resurrection means sin and death do not possess ultimate authorship over those who belong to Him.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same truth:
From scandal to grace... because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history into a lie.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He rewrites the ending.
He takes Peter's denial and makes him a preacher.
He takes Saul the persecutor and makes him Paul the apostle.
He takes sinners and makes them saints—not because their sins were imaginary, but because His blood is sufficient.
And He took Mary Magdalene, delivered her from terrible spiritual bondage, and placed her where the Gospel writers could never erase her:
near the cross...
near the tomb...
and face-to-face with the risen Christ.
Then He sent her with news.
That is the detail I cannot stop thinking about.
Jesus entrusted resurrection news to Mary.
The first Easter morning did not begin with Mary defending her reputation.
It began with Mary discovering that Jesus was alive.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs today.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life defending yourself before every person committed to misunderstanding you.
Follow Christ.
Tell the truth.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is commanded.
Make restitution where restitution is possible.
Walk humbly.
And let the fruit of a transformed life speak.
Mary did not need to spend Easter morning explaining who she wasn't.
She had something infinitely greater to say:
I have seen the Lord.
And that should confront us.
Because Christianity was never meant to become an endless fascination with somebody else's scandal.
It is supposed to be an encounter with the risen Jesus that sends redeemed people into the world with good news.
So be honest for a moment.
What name have you been carrying that Jesus never gave you?
What accusation still controls you?
What sin have you confessed to God but continue wearing as though Christ's blood were insufficient?
Or perhaps the harder question:
Whom have you frozen inside an old reputation?
Whose worst chapter have you kept rereading after God may have begun writing something new?
Whose story have you repeated without knowing whether it was true?
Mary Magdalene's distorted reputation should make Christians very careful with another person's name.
A rumor repeated for long enough does not become Scripture.
A tradition repeated for centuries does not become a verse.
And an accusation believed by millions does not become truth simply because millions believed it.
Truth still matters.
Grace still matters.
Names still matter.
People still matter.
And Jesus still calls people out of darkness.
Be honest.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
Someone still chained to an old name.
Someone convinced that what they did is greater than what Jesus did at Calvary.
There may come a night when the old accusations become loud again.
Come back and remember Mary standing in a garden, crying because she thought everything was over...
until Jesus spoke her name.
It doesn't.
Not because Christians can purchase blessing.
They cannot.
Give freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and according to Scripture.
But there is something remarkably fitting about this particular story.
Luke does not merely tell us that Mary Magdalene and other women followed Jesus. He tells us that women associated with His ministry supported the work from their own resources.
Their possessions became instruments of Kingdom service.
And believers can still choose to do something similar today.
But the deeper reason to stay connected isn't merchandise.
Look back to Jesus.
Return to Scripture.
Don't make peace with sin.
Don't surrender to shame.
Keep following Christ.
Think about Jesus.
Because He is the center of her story.
He is the One who delivered her.
He is the One she followed.
He is the One she watched die.
He is the One she searched for.
He is the One who rose.
He is the One who called her name.
He is the One she proclaimed.
And He is still the only One who can save us.
Mary Magdalene does not need us to turn her into a prostitute so grace can look beautiful.
Calvary already showed us how beautiful grace is.
The empty tomb already showed us how powerful Jesus is.
And perhaps Mary Magdalene's true story leaves us with something even more haunting than the legend ever could:
For centuries, people remembered her by a scandal Scripture never gave her...
while Scripture remembered her standing near an empty tomb telling the world that Jesus was alive.
So before you allow another person's accusation—or even your own past—to write the final sentence over your life, remember the woman crying in the garden.
Remember the voice behind her.
Remember the moment He said her name.
Because when Jesus Christ becomes the Author of your redemption, the grave doesn't get the last word.
Neither does your scandal.
